properties.description:
The first measured prioritisation of reflow2's own tool surface, and the first repair driven by the usage ledger shipped in v0.59.0.

WHAT PROMPTED IT: Anthony observed, unmeasured, that "some tools take a long time — I think one takes 12.5s" and asked for a campaign ranking tools by how often they are used. The ledger made that rankable for the first time. loop_status was 71.4% of all time spent inside reflow2 (604 s of 846 s across 150 calls), at a median of 12,089 ms — and his 12.5 s estimate was accurate.

WHAT THE INVESTIGATION FOUND, and it inverted the plan: the baseline is 1,284 ms, not 12 s. Four hypotheses were falsified by measurement (debug binary, shared-daemon transport, RocksDB compaction debt, and the instrument itself). The 12 s is three measured amplifiers — a per-write memo invalidation (x3.2), concurrency (x1.6 at four clients) and machine load (up to x6). And 32 of 39 calls came from the Stop/PostToolUse probe rather than from the agent, fourteen of them in same-second pairs.

WHAT THIS EPOCH CONTAINS: the duplicate hook registration removed, and the probe's check-then-write guard replaced with an atomic claim — the class fix, since PostToolUse and Stop can legitimately arrive together even with one registration. Plus a second latency budget for the path a working session actually takes, and the correction of a stale budget edge that had been reporting `exceeded` on a budget that held.

WHAT IT MUST NOT BE READ AS: the budget is NOT met. This epoch reduces how OFTEN the expensive rollup runs; it does not make it faster. 4,096 ms against a 1,000 ms limit stands, and the two levers that would close it — the write-tax and the intrinsic scan cost — were left unstarted and need their own ruling.
properties.name: The loop check stops firing twice — the first usage ledger prices a "wasted read" at 71% of all tool time, and the guard that was supposed to stop it was never atomic (2026-09-12)
